div.head: Chapter 25
div.p: It was stated in the conclusion that each of those who were present there is bound in solidum — meaning each one for the whole or for all —: this is proved by that maxim of Saint Thomas 2.2 q. 62 a. 7: "Whoever is the cause of an unjust taking or of damage is bound to make restitution." For all those hundred and seventy soulless men were jointly the total cause of the seizure and death and robbery of that king, and of seven or eight thousand unarmed men whom they killed there that day — those who were carrying the king in his litter or on their shoulders — and afterwards of many more; and none of them — not ten, not twenty, not thirty — would have dared to go to those kingdoms or to undertake what they did; and so, all of them attacked, all of them seized, all of them killed, and all of them robbed and usurped those kingdoms. And this is one reason.

Another reason is that all and each of them went and acted with the same knowledge and the same desire, because all knew and wanted and wished to go for what they were going for, and went with the same purpose and the same intention, with the same ambition and greed; namely, to make war and subjugate and lord it over and rob those kingdoms and peoples who had never done them harm or injury or wrong, nor wronged or offended them, nor deserved ill from them. And so they robbed them of their gold, their silver, their infinite riches, their lands, their kingdoms, their estates, despoiling them of their liberty and of their kingdoms and lordships. And amid all of this, those very men and those who came after them burned people alive and killed them with diverse and immense forms of torment, and cast them into hell without faith and without sacraments. Therefore all and each of them are bound to restore everything they robbed and tyrannized, and to satisfy for the immense harms that since that time multiplied throughout all those kingdoms.

This consequence is proved: first, because "the obligation to make restitution follows causally upon the act of taking or causing harm; and this in the present case belongs to those whose actions and deeds extend to taking all things and inflicting all harms, and who are the direct and sole cause of the will and operation by which the whole good is taken away and the whole harm inflicted, even though each may have been a partial cause. And thus their causality extends to the whole. And therefore each is liable for the whole, which is what is meant by in solidum, since together they were the total cause of those harms, even though individually each was a partial cause, being by himself the cause of the whole taking done or harm given." As is clear from L. ita vulneratus, §. fin., ff., Ad Legem Aquiliam; et L. si plures, Digest., Arborum furtim scisarum.

The second is proved by the law that says: "If several persons knocked down a beam and it crushed someone, all of them are liable under the Lex Aquilia." L. item mela, §. si plures, ff., Ad Legem Aquiliam.

The third, from L. vulgaris, §. Si duo. ff. De furtis, where it says thus: "If two or more persons stole a beam that none of them could carry alone: it must be said that all of them are liable for theft in solidum; even though no one of them could handle or carry it alone: and this is our practice, for it cannot be said that each of them stole only a part, but rather that all stole the whole thing. And so it results that each is liable for the theft." Thus far there. And in the said §. fin. it says thus: "When several persons lifted a beam belonging to another with intent to steal it, a beam that none of them could carry alone, it is held that all of them are liable for the action of theft." Thus far there. And in the gloss there it is said that all are liable in solidum. And the said L. vulgaris, penúlt. is cited. For there are as many offenses as there are persons, as in ff., De injuriis, L. si plures; et gloss in L. 1, Si plures, ff., De eo per quem factum erit.

Those hundred and seventy are therefore bound, each one in solidum, for everything they robbed, and to satisfy for all the harms they did while they lived, and to restore and satisfy everything that those who came afterwards to those kingdoms robbed and the harms they did to all those peoples, because it has been proved that they opened the gate and were the occasion of all the robberies and evils that afterwards befell those kingdoms and peoples.

What follows in the conclusion is that they were faithless, as men without faith and without truth and unworthy of being called men: which is proved because even toward enemies and those against whom we wage just war, we are bound to keep and fulfill the faith and word we have pledged; and "it is against natural equity not to keep one's agreements," as in L. Conventionum, f., De pactis; et L. postliminium, inducit, et L. Non dubito, ff. de captivis et postlimiis. And as appears from c. Nola, 23, q. 1, et gloss in c. utilem, 22, q. 27 and Saint Thomas, 2.2 q. 40 a. 3 corp.: "For there are certain rights of war and compacts that must be observed even between enemies themselves, as Ambrose says in his book On Offices." How much more were they bound to keep and fulfill the faith and promise they made him to release him from so unjust an imprisonment! For he fulfilled what he had promised them and more than what he had promised, in giving them as much gold and silver as could fill a room five or six stories high, adding half a story more above the mark they had set for him. Still more so because even had they released him, they were still bound to restore the roomful of gold to the last farthing, because the imprisonment was unjust and tyrannical, and while in prison, promising all he had, any agreement made was invalid, as is manifest to those who know anything of the laws. See the L. decernimus and what is noted there, which we cited in § 4.

They were therefore faithless and without faith or truth, and a great ignominy to the honor of God and the Christian religion. In what esteem would that king hold, from that point forward — since they did not burn him —, the faith and word of Christians? Finally, it appears plain — and more than plain — what most grave sins those men committed against God and against men, and what obligation those of them who are now dead had, and those who remain still have, to restore that ransom and everything else. And because neither those who died made restitution nor showed any sign of penitence, without doubt they are burning today in hell; and of those who still live today, no compunction or repentance whatsoever is felt for their inexplicable and most wicked sins; rather they glory in them; and for restitution they have, as appears and we see, no concern whatsoever. Therefore no doubt should be entertained that they will go where the others are waiting for them. And so the conclusion, as we believe, stands well proved.
